reference_solution: WITH eligible_users AS (SELECT user_id, cohort_week FROM users WHERE is_test = FALSE), deduplicated_activity AS (SELECT DISTINCT source_event_id, user_id, activity_week, event_name FROM activity), retained_users AS (SELECT DISTINCT u.user_id, u.cohort_week FROM eligible_users AS u JOIN deduplicated_activity AS a ON a.user_id = u.user_id AND a.activity_week = u.cohort_week + 1 AND a.event_name = 'session_started') SELECT u.cohort_week, COUNT(*) AS users, COUNT(r.user_id) AS retained_week_one FROM eligible_users AS u LEFT JOIN retained_users AS r ON r.user_id = u.user_id AND r.cohort_week = u.cohort_week GROUP BY u.cohort_week ORDER BY u.cohort_week;
explanation: The solution establishes the denominator first by filtering out test accounts. It then removes repeated source deliveries using source_event_id before evaluating retention. A second DISTINCT reduces qualifying activity to one retained row per user and cohort, so multiple legitimate sessions still count once. The final LEFT JOIN preserves cohorts with no qualifying week-one activity, and COUNT(r.user_id) returns zero for those cohorts. The explicit activity_week = cohort_week + 1 condition prevents later activity from being counted as week-one retention.

alternatives.name: Conditional distinct aggregation
alternatives.solution: Join eligible users to deduplicated qualifying activity and use COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN activity_week = cohort_week + 1 THEN user_id END).
advantages: can be convenient for adding several retention windows
disadvantages: harder to audit when more dimensions and event filters are added

alternatives.name: Incremental retained-user fact table
alternatives.solution: Materialize one row per user, cohort, and retained week offset after source-event deduplication, then aggregate the fact table for reporting.
advantages: avoids rescanning the full event stream
supports repeated cohort reporting and retention matrices
disadvantages: requires late-event reconciliation and backfill ownership

trade_off_analysis: The staged CTE form prioritizes correctness and auditability over minimizing query text.
COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) can protect the final count, but source-event deduplication remains valuable for data-quality observability and future metrics that are event-based.
At large scale, activity should be partitioned by reporting date or week and clustered or indexed on the retained-window join keys; repeatedly scanning all historical activity is not acceptable.
Late events require a bounded cohort-recomputation window or an incremental correction process rather than assuming published cohorts never change.

complexity.expected_time: O(U + A_q) logical work for eligible users U and qualifying activity rows A_q after partition pruning; physical cost depends on indexes, partitions, and deduplication strategy.
complexity.expected_space: O(D + R) working state for deduplicated source events D and retained users R, subject to PostgreSQL hash/sort spill behavior.
complexity.explanation: A production plan should prune activity to the relevant week range, avoid a global historical DISTINCT, and monitor sort/hash spills and cardinality estimates.

testing_and_debugging: Start with a cohort that has no activity and verify it remains with retained_week_one = 0.
Replay one source_event_id several times and verify the retained count does not change.
Give one user several distinct week-one sessions and verify that user still counts once.
Add page views, test users, and sessions from weeks zero and two to verify exclusion rules.
Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on production-shaped data to confirm partition pruning and detect spills or row-estimate errors.
production_follow_ups: Add a uniqueness or replay-monitoring control for source_event_id at the ingestion or curated-event layer.
Partition activity by event/reporting date and index or cluster on activity_week, event_name, and user_id according to observed selectivity.
Materialize retained-user facts incrementally and recompute a bounded late-arrival window.
Publish denominator, numerator, late-arrival adjustment, duplicate-rate, and freshness checks alongside the metric.
critical_omissions: Dropping cohorts with no retained users through an inner join.
Counting activity rows instead of distinct retained users.
Including test accounts, wrong event types, or activity outside the exact following week.
Assuming at-least-once source delivery cannot replay events.
Claiming production scalability without a partition, index, incremental-computation, and late-arrival plan.
strong_response_example: I will first define the eligible cohort denominator, then deduplicate source events, reduce qualifying week-one sessions to one row per user, and left join that retained-user set back to the cohort population. This preserves zero-retention cohorts and prevents both replayed events and multiple sessions from inflating the numerator. For production scale I would prune by reporting week, inspect the execution plan, materialize retained-user facts incrementally, and recompute a bounded late-arrival window while monitoring replay rate and metric freshness.
